name: Chapter 3: Matrices
description: Order and types of matrices, equality, addition and scalar multiplication, matrix multiplication, transpose, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices, invertible matrices, and exam-style problems.

cards.term: Define a matrix.
cards.definition:
An ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions.
The numbers are its elements (entries).
Horizontal lines are rows, vertical lines are columns

cards.term: What is the order of a matrix? How many elements?
cards.definition: m rows and n columns: order m × n (“m by n”), with mn elements. Rows come first, then columns

cards.term: What does aᵢⱼ mean?
cards.definition:
The element in the i-th row and j-th column.
i-th row: (aᵢ₁, ..., aᵢₙ)
j-th column: (a₁ⱼ, ..., aₘⱼ)

cards.term: Example 2: if a matrix has 8 elements, what orders are possible?
cards.definition: All pairs of natural numbers with product 8: 1 × 8, 8 × 1, 2 × 4, 4 × 2

cards.term: How do you find all possible orders for a matrix with N elements?
cards.definition: List the ordered factor pairs (m, n) with mn = N. A prime N (like 13 or 5) gives only 1 × N and N × 1

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q1: for A =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 5 & 19 & -7 \\[0.7em] 35 & -2 & \dfrac{5}{2} & 12 \\[0.7em] \sqrt{3} & 1 & -5 & 17\end{bmatrix}\]find the order, number of elements, a₁₃, a₂₁, a₃₃, a₂₄, a₂₃.
cards.definition: Order 3 × 4, 12 elements. a₁₃ = 19, a₂₁ = 35, a₃₃ = −5, a₂₄ = 12, a₂₃ = 5/2

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q2: possible orders for 24 elements? for 13 elements?
Ex 3.1 Q3: possible orders for 18 elements? for 5 elements?
Ex 3.1 Q4(i): build the 2 × 2 matrix with aᵢⱼ = (i + j)²/2.
cards.definition: a₁₁ = 2, a₁₂ = 9/2, a₂₁ = 9/2, a₂₂ = 8:\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & \dfrac{9}{2} \\[0.7em] \dfrac{9}{2} & 8\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q4(ii),(iii): 2 × 2 with aᵢⱼ = i/j, and with aᵢⱼ = (i + 2j)²/2.
cards.definition: (ii)\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & \dfrac{1}{2} \\[0.7em] 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\](iii) a₁₁ = 9/2, a₁₂ = 25/2, a₂₁ = 8, a₂₂ = 18:\[\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{9}{2} & \dfrac{25}{2} \\[0.7em] 8 & 18\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q5: build the 3 × 4 matrices with (i) aᵢⱼ = ½|−3i + j| and (ii) aᵢⱼ = 2i − j.
How are the vertices of a polygon written as a matrix?
cards.definition: Each vertex (x, y) is a row [x y] (or a column). ABCD with A(1,0), B(3,2), C(1,3), D(−1,2) is a 4 × 2 matrix with rows [1 0], [3 2], [1 3], [−1 2]. Transformations (rotation, reflection) are then matrix multiplications

cards.term: Types of matrices
cards.definition: Column matrix: only one column (m × 1); Row matrix: only one row (1 × n); Square matrix: rows = columns (n × n); diagonal a₁₁, a₂₂, …, aₙₙ; Diagonal matrix: square, aᵢⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j; Scalar matrix: diagonal with all diagonal entries equal (k); Identity matrix Iₙ: diagonal with all diagonal entries 1; Zero matrix O: all elements 0 (any order)

Types of matrices

Define each type of matrix.

Column matrixonly one column (m × 1)
Row matrixonly one row (1 × n)
Square matrixrows = columns (n × n); diagonal a₁₁, a₂₂, …, aₙₙ
Diagonal matrixsquare, aᵢⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j
Scalar matrixdiagonal with all diagonal entries equal (k)
Identity matrix Iₙdiagonal with all diagonal entries 1
Zero matrix Oall elements 0 (any order)

Identity ⊂ scalar ⊂ diagonal ⊂ square

cards.term: How are identity, scalar and diagonal matrices related?
cards.definition:
Identity ⊂ scalar ⊂ diagonal ⊂ square
Every identity matrix is scalar (k = 1).
Every scalar matrix is diagonal.
But a diagonal matrix like diag(1, 2) is not scalar

cards.term: Is a zero matrix a square matrix? Is it a diagonal matrix?
cards.definition: A zero matrix can have any order. If it is square it is also diagonal and scalar (k = 0), but not an identity matrix

cards.term: Define equal matrices.
cards.definition: Same order and aᵢⱼ = bᵢⱼ for every position.\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \neq \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]because the orders differ

cards.term: Example 4: two equal 3 × 3 matrices give x + 3 = 0, z + 4 = 6, 2y − 7 = 3y − 2, a − 1 = −3, 0 = 2c + 2, b − 3 = 2b + 4. Solve.
cards.definition: Each equation has one unknown: x = −3, z = 2, y = −5, a = −2, c = −1, b = −7

cards.term: Example 5:\[\begin{bmatrix}2a + b & a - 2b \\ 5c - d & 4c + 3d\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4 & -3 \\ 11 & 24\end{bmatrix}\]Find a, b, c, d.
cards.definition: Two systems: 2a + b = 4, a − 2b = −3 give a = 1, b = 2; 5c − d = 11, 4c + 3d = 24 give c = 3, d = 4

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q6(i):\[\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ x & 5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}y & z \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: Equal entries:\[y = 4, z = 3, x = 1\]

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q6(ii):\[\begin{bmatrix}x + y & 2 \\ 5 + z & xy\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 5 & 8\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: z = 0, x + y = 6, xy = 8: x, y are 2 and 4 in either order: (x, y, z) = (2, 4, 0) or (4, 2, 0)

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q6(iii): column (x + y + z, x + z, y + z) = (9, 5, 7).
cards.definition: Subtract: y = 9 − 5 = 4, x = 9 − 7 = 2, z = 3:\[x = 2, y = 4, z = 3\]

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q7:\[\begin{bmatrix}a - b & 2a + c \\ 2a - b & 3c + d\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 \\ 0 & 13\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: a − b = −1 and 2a − b = 0 give a = 1, b = 2. Then 2 + c = 5 gives c = 3; 9 + d = 13 gives d = 4:\[a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4\]

cards.term:
Ex 3.1 Q8: A = [aᵢⱼ]ₘₓₙ is a square matrix if
(A) m < n (B) m > n
(C) m = n
(D) none
cards.definition: (C) m = n

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q9: for which x, y are\[\begin{bmatrix}3x + 7 & 5 \\ y + 1 & 2 - 3x\end{bmatrix}\]and\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & y - 2 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]equal?
cards.definition: x = −7/3 and y = 7 from the first row and first column, but then 2 − 3x = 9 ≠ 4. Not possible (B)

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q10: number of 3 × 3 matrices with each entry 0 or 1?
cards.definition: Nine entries, two choices each: 2⁹ = 512 (D)

cards.term: When can two matrices be added? How?
cards.definition: Only when they have the same order. Add corresponding entries: (A + B)ᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ + bᵢⱼ

cards.term: Multiplication of a matrix by a scalar k?
cards.definition: kA = [k aᵢⱼ]: multiply every element by k. −A = (−1)A, and A − B = A + (−1)B (same order needed)

cards.term: Properties of matrix addition?
cards.definition: Commutative A + B = B + A associative (A + B) + C = A + (B + C) additive identity O (A + O = A) additive inverse −A (A + (−A) = O)

cards.term: Properties of scalar multiplication?
cards.definition: k(A + B) = kA + kB and (k + l)A = kA + lA (also k(lA) = (kl)A and 1·A = A)

cards.term: Example 9: X + Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}\]and X − Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]Find X and Y.
cards.definition: Add: 2X =\[\begin{bmatrix}8 & 8 \\ 0 & 8\end{bmatrix}\]so X =\[\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]Subtract: 2Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 10\end{bmatrix}\]so Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Method: solve 2A + 3X = 5B for X.
cards.definition:
3X = 5B − 2A, so X = (1/3)(5B − 2A)
Treat matrix equations like algebra, but never divide by a matrix: multiply by scalars only

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q1: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]C =\[\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]Find A + B, A − B, 3A − C.
cards.definition: A + B =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 1 & 7\end{bmatrix}\]A − B =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 5 & -3\end{bmatrix}\]3A − C =\[\begin{bmatrix}6 + 2 & 12 - 5 \\ 9 - 3 & 6 - 4\end{bmatrix}\]=\[\begin{bmatrix}8 & 7 \\ 6 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q2(i),(ii):\[\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ -b & a\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}\]and\[\begin{bmatrix}a^{2} + b^{2} & b^{2} + c^{2} \\ a^{2} + c^{2} & a^{2} + b^{2}\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}2ab & 2bc \\ -2ac & -2ab\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: (i)\[\begin{bmatrix}2a & 2b \\ 0 & 2a\end{bmatrix}\](ii)\[\begin{bmatrix}(a + b)^{2} & (b + c)^{2} \\ (a - c)^{2} & (a - b)^{2}\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term:
Ex 3.2 Q2(iii),(iv):
(iii)\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 & -6 \\ 8 & 5 & 16 \\ 2 & 8 & 5\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}12 & 7 & 6 \\ 8 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\](iv)\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos ^{2}x & \sin ^{2}x \\ \sin ^{2}x & \cos ^{2}x\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}\sin ^{2}x & \cos ^{2}x \\ \cos ^{2}x & \sin ^{2}x\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: (iii)\[\begin{bmatrix}11 & 11 & 0 \\ 16 & 5 & 21 \\ 5 & 10 & 9\end{bmatrix}\](iv) every entry is cos²x + sin²x = 1:\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q4: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 5 \\ 2 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]C =\[\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]Find A + B and B − C.
cards.definition: A + B =\[\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 & -1 \\ 9 & 2 & 7 \\ 3 & -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]B − C =\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]Then A + (B − C) = (A + B) − C by associativity

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q5: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{2}{3} & 1 & \dfrac{5}{3} \\[0.7em] \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{4}{3} \\[0.7em] \dfrac{7}{3} & 2 & \dfrac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5} & 1 \\[0.7em] \dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{4}{5} \\[0.7em] \dfrac{7}{5} & \dfrac{6}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5}\end{bmatrix}\]Compute 3A − 5B.
cards.definition: Each entry: 3aᵢⱼ − 5bᵢⱼ = 0 (for example 3·2/3 − 5·2/5 = 0): the 3 × 3 zero matrix

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q6: simplify\[\cos  \theta \begin{bmatrix}\cos  \theta & \sin  \theta \\ -\sin  \theta & \cos  \theta\end{bmatrix} + \sin  \theta \begin{bmatrix}\sin  \theta & -\cos  \theta \\ \cos  \theta & \sin  \theta\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: Top-left cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, top-right cosθ sinθ − sinθ cosθ = 0, and so on: I =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q7(i): X + Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]and X − Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]Find X, Y.
cards.definition: X = ½(sum + difference) =\[\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]Y = ½(sum − difference) =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q7(ii): 2X + 3Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]and 3X + 2Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]Find X, Y.
cards.definition: Eliminate: X = (3Q − 2P)/5 and Y = (3P − 2Q)/5 where P, Q are the two right-hand sides. That gives X =\[\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{2}{5} & -\dfrac{12}{5} \\[0.7em] -\dfrac{11}{5} & 3\end{bmatrix}\]and Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{13}{5} \\[0.7em] \dfrac{14}{5} & -2\end{bmatrix}\]Check: 2X + 3Y top-left = 4/5 + 6/5 = 2 ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q8: Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]and 2X + Y =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]Find X.
cards.definition: 2X =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 - 3 & 0 - 2 \\ -3 - 1 & 2 - 4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\]X =\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q9:\[2 \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & x\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}y & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 \\ 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}\]Find x, y.
cards.definition: LHS =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 + y & 6 \\ 1 & 2x + 2\end{bmatrix}\]So y = 3 and 2x + 2 = 8: x = 3, y = 3

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q10:\[2 \begin{bmatrix}x & z \\ y & t\end{bmatrix} + 3 \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} = 3 \begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]Solve.

cards.definition: 2x − y = 10 and 3x + y = 5. Add: 5x = 15:\[x = 3, y = -4\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q12:\[3 \begin{bmatrix}x & y \\ z & w\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}x & 6 \\ -1 & 2w\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}4 & x + y \\ z + w & 3\end{bmatrix}\]
When is the product AB defined, and what is its order?
cards.definition: When columns of A = rows of B. For A (m × n) and B (n × p): AB is m × p

cards.term: Order of a matrix product: inner numbers match, outer numbers remain
cards.definition: (m x n)(n x p) = (m x p): number of columns of A must equal number of rows of B; AB may exist while BA does not

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Matrix multiplication · orders

A has order 2 × 3 and B has order 3 × 4. Is AB defined? Is BA? What is the order of the product?

Compare the columns of A with the rows of B.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Matrix multiplication · orders

A has order 2 × 3 and B has order 3 × 4. Is AB defined? Is BA? What is the order of the product?

(m × n)(n × p) = (m × p): the inner numbers must match; the outer numbers give the order.

AB is 2 × 4. BA would need 4 = 2, so BA is not defined. Both AB and BA exist only if A is m × n and B is n × m; then AB is m × m and BA is n × n.

cards.term: Matrix product: row of A times column of B
cards.definition: Entry (i,j) of AB = sum over k of a_ik b_kj (row i of A dot column j of B); AB for A=[[2,4],[3,2]], B=[[1,3],[-2,5]] is [[-6,26],[-1,19]]

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Matrix multiplication · row × column

Multiply A = [[2, 4], [3, 2]] and B = [[1, 3], [−2, 5]]. How is each entry of AB built?

Walk along a row of A and down a column of B.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Matrix multiplication · row × column

Multiply A = [[2, 4], [3, 2]] and B = [[1, 3], [−2, 5]]. How is each entry of AB built?

The (i, j) entry of AB is row i of A times column j of B, multiplied term by term and added: cᵢⱼ = Σ aᵢₖ bₖⱼ.

AB = [[2·1 + 4(−2), 2·3 + 4·5], [3·1 + 2(−2), 3·3 + 2·5]] = [[−6, 26], [−1, 19]] (Ex 3.2 Q1(iv)). Note BA = [[11, 10], [11, 2]] is different.

cards.term: Formula for the (i, k) entry of AB?
cards.definition: cᵢₖ = aᵢ₁b₁ₖ + aᵢ₂b₂ₖ + ... + aᵢₙbₙₖ = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ bⱼₖ: row i of A dotted with column k of B

cards.term: Example 12: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}6 & 9 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 0 \\ 7 & 9 & 8\end{bmatrix}\]Find AB. Is BA defined?
cards.definition: AB is 2 × 3:\[\begin{bmatrix}75 & 117 & 72 \\ 25 & 39 & 24\end{bmatrix}\]BA: B has 3 columns but A has 2 rows: not defined

cards.term: If AB is defined, is BA defined? When are both defined?
cards.definition: Not necessarily. For A (m × n), B (k × l): both AB and BA exist iff n = k and l = m. For square matrices of the same order both always exist

cards.term: Is matrix multiplication commutative?
cards.definition: No: AB ≠ BA in general (they may even have different orders). Example 14: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]give AB =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]but BA =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: When is AB = BA guaranteed?
cards.definition: Diagonal matrices of the same order commute. Also A commutes with I, O, and any scalar matrix kI, with itself and its powers, and with polynomials in A

cards.term: Example 15: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]Find AB. What does it show?
cards.definition: AB = O. So AB = O does not imply A = O or B = O (real numbers behave differently)

cards.term: Trap: does AB = AC imply B = C?
cards.definition: No (no cancellation law). A(B − C) = O does not force B = C when A ≠ O. Example: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]C =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]give AB = AC

cards.term: Properties of matrix multiplication?
cards.definition: Associative (AB)C = A(BC) distributive A(B + C) = AB + AC and (A + B)C = AC + BC identity IA = AI = A but not commutative

cards.term: Trap: (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B²?
cards.definition:
Not in general.
(A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², and AB ≠ BA.
It holds only when AB = BA.
Likewise (AB)² ≠ A²B² and A² − B² ≠ (A − B)(A + B) in general

cards.term: Example 19: cost per contact A = [40, 100, 50]ᵀ paise; contacts X: [1000, 500, 5000], Y: [3000, 1000, 10000]. Total cost for each city?
cards.definition:
City X: 40 000 + 50 000 + 250 000 = 340 000 paise
City Y: 120 000 + 100 000 + 500 000 = 720 000 paise
That is ₹3400 and ₹7200

cards.term: Example 18: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]Show A³ − 23A − 40I = O.
cards.definition:
A² =\[\begin{bmatrix}19 & 4 & 8 \\ 1 & 12 & 8 \\ 14 & 6 & 15\end{bmatrix}\]A³ =\[\begin{bmatrix}63 & 46 & 69 \\ 69 & -6 & 23 \\ 92 & 46 & 63\end{bmatrix}\]Then A³ − 23A − 40I = O entry by entry.
(Cayley–Hamilton: a matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation)

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q1(iv),(v): AB and BA for A =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: AB =\[\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 26 \\ -1 & 19\end{bmatrix}\]and BA =\[\begin{bmatrix}11 & 10 \\ 11 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]Different, so AB ≠ BA

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q3(i):\[\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ -b & a\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: Top-left a² + b², top-right −ab + ab = 0, bottom-left −ab + ab = 0, bottom-right b² + a²: (a² + b²) I

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q3(ii): the column [1, 2, 3]ᵀ times the row [2, 3, 4].
cards.definition: A 3 × 1 times a 1 × 3 gives a 3 × 3 (outer product):\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 4 \\ 4 & 6 & 8 \\ 6 & 9 & 12\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q3(iii):\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: 2 × 2 by 2 × 3 is 2 × 3:\[\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 13 & 9\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q3(iv):\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 4 & 5 & 6\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: \[\begin{bmatrix}14 & 0 & 42 \\ 18 & -1 & 56 \\ 22 & -2 & 70\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q3(v):\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: 3 × 2 by 2 × 3 is 3 × 3:\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \\ -2 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q3(vi):\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 3 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: 2 × 3 by 3 × 2 is 2 × 2:\[\begin{bmatrix}14 & -6 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q13: F(x) =\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos  x & -\sin  x & 0 \\ \sin  x & \cos  x & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]Show F(x)F(y) = F(x + y).
cards.definition: Top-left: cos x cos y − sin x sin y = cos(x + y) top-right: −cos x sin y − sin x cos y = −sin(x + y) and so on. Rotations about the z-axis compose by adding angles

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q14(i): show\[\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix} \neq \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: Left:\[\begin{bmatrix}7 & 1 \\ 33 & 34\end{bmatrix}\]Right:\[\begin{bmatrix}16 & 5 \\ 39 & 25\end{bmatrix}\]Different

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q14(ii): the 3 × 3 non-commutativity example.
cards.definition: One order gives\[\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 & 14 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]the other\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 11 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]not equal

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q15: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]Find A² − 5A + 6I.
cards.definition: A² =\[\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 & 2 \\ 9 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\]Then A² − 5A + 6I =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -3 \\ -1 & -1 & -10 \\ -5 & 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q16: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]Prove A³ − 6A² + 7A + 2I = O.
cards.definition: Compute A² and A³, then combine entry by entry: every entry cancels to 0. ✓ (Cayley–Hamilton again)

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q17: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\]Find k with A² = kA − 2I.
cards.definition: A² =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 4 & -4\end{bmatrix}\]and kA − 2I =\[\begin{bmatrix}3k - 2 & -2k \\ 4k & -2k - 2\end{bmatrix}\]Then k = 1 fits every entry: k = 1

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q18: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & -\tan (\alpha /2) \\ \tan (\alpha /2) & 0\end{bmatrix}\]Show I + A = (I − A)\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos  \alpha & -\sin  \alpha \\ \sin  \alpha & \cos  \alpha\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: With t = tan(α/2): cos α = (1 − t²)/(1 + t²), sin α = 2t/(1 + t²). Multiply out (I − A)(rotation) =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & t \\ -t & 1\end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix}\cos \alpha & -\sin \alpha \\ \sin \alpha & \cos \alpha\end{bmatrix}\]and simplify to\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -t \\ t & 1\end{bmatrix}\]= I + A. ✓

cards.term:
Ex 3.2 Q19: ₹30 000 is split between bonds paying 5% and 7%. How much in each to earn
(a) ₹1800
(b) ₹2000?
cards.definition: Let x and 30 000 − x: 0.05x + 0.07(30 000 − x) = interest. (a) 2100 − 0.02x = 1800 gives ₹15 000 and ₹15 000. (b) 2100 − 0.02x = 2000 gives ₹5 000 and ₹25 000

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q20: 10 dozen chemistry books at ₹80, 8 dozen physics at ₹60, 10 dozen economics at ₹40. Total receipts?
cards.definition: Quantities (120, 96, 120) times prices (80, 60, 40): 9600 + 5760 + 4800 = ₹20 160

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q21: X is 2 × n, Y is 3 × k, Z is 2 × p, W is n × 3, P is p × k. When is PY + WY defined?
cards.definition: PY = (p × k)(3 × k) needs k = 3 and then has order p × 3. WY = (n × 3)(3 × k) has order n × 3. To add them the orders must agree: p = n. (A) k = 3, p = n

cards.term:
Ex 3.2 Q22: if n = p, the order of 7X − 5Z is
(A) p × 2
(B) 2 × n
(C) n × 3
(D) p × n
cards.definition: X is 2 × n and Z is 2 × p = 2 × n, so the combination is (B) 2 × n

cards.term: Define the transpose of a matrix.
cards.definition: A′ (or Aᵀ): swap rows and columns. If A is m × n then A′ is n × m and (A′)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ

cards.term: Properties of the transpose?
cards.definition: (A′)′ = A, (kA)′ = kA′, (A + B)′ = A′ + B′, (AB)′ = B′A′ (order reverses, like socks and shoes)

cards.term: Trap: (AB)′ = A′B′?
cards.definition:
No. It is B′A′.
A′B′ may not even be defined.
A (2 × 3), B (3 × 4): (AB)′ is 4 × 2 = (4 × 3)(3 × 2) = B′A′

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q1: transposes of the column [5, 1/2, −1]ᵀ, of\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]and of\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 & 6 \\ \sqrt{3} & 5 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: (i) the row [5, 1/2, −1]. (ii)\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\](iii)\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & \sqrt{3} & 2 \\ 5 & 5 & 3 \\ 6 & 6 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q4: A′ =\[\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]and B =\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]Find (A + 2B)′.
cards.definition: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]A + 2B =\[\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 5 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]transpose\[\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 5 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]Or use (A + 2B)′ = A′ + 2B′
AB =\[\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & -8 & -4 \\ -3 & 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\](3 × 3); its transpose equals B′A′ = the column [−1, 2, 1]ᵀ times the row [1, −4, 3]. ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q6: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos  \alpha & \sin  \alpha \\ -\sin  \alpha & \cos  \alpha\end{bmatrix}\]Verify A′A = I.
cards.definition: A′A =\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos ^{2}\alpha + \sin ^{2}\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & \sin ^{2}\alpha + \cos ^{2}\alpha\end{bmatrix}\]= I (A is an orthogonal / rotation matrix: A′ = A⁻¹)

cards.term: Define symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices.
cards.definition: Symmetric: A′ = A (aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ). Skew-symmetric: A′ = −A (aⱼᵢ = −aᵢⱼ). Both must be square

cards.term: Symmetric vs skew-symmetric: mirror in the diagonal
cards.definition: Symmetric: A^T = A, a_ij = a_ji. Skew-symmetric: A^T = -A, a_ji = -a_ij and the diagonal is zero

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Symmetric and skew-symmetric

Look at the entries of P and Q. Which one is symmetric and which is skew-symmetric? What pattern defines each?

Reflect each matrix in its main diagonal.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Symmetric and skew-symmetric

Look at the entries of P and Q. Which one is symmetric and which is skew-symmetric? What pattern defines each?

Symmetric (P′ = P): aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ. Mirror the matrix in the main diagonal and nothing changes.

Skew-symmetric (Q′ = −Q): aⱼᵢ = −aᵢⱼ. Mirrored entries are opposites, and since aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ every diagonal entry is 0.

cards.term: Why is every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix 0?
cards.definition: aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ ⇒ 2aᵢᵢ = 0 ⇒ aᵢᵢ = 0

cards.term: Theorem 1: what do you know about A + A′ and A − A′ for a square matrix A?
cards.definition: A + A′ is symmetric and A − A′ is skew-symmetric ((A + A′)′ = A′ + A; (A − A′)′ = A′ − A = −(A − A′))

cards.term: Theorem 2: express any square matrix as symmetric + skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: A = ½(A + A′) + ½(A − A′). The decomposition is unique

cards.term: Can a matrix be both symmetric and skew-symmetric?
cards.definition: Only the zero matrix (A′ = A = −A ⇒ A = O). That is Misc Q10: answer (B) zero matrix

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q7: show\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]is symmetric and\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]is skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: First: equals its transpose (mirror entries match: −1, 5, 1). Second: zero diagonal and mirror entries are opposites: 1 vs −1, −1 vs 1, 1 vs −1. ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q8: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}\]Verify A + A′ is symmetric and A − A′ is skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: A + A′ =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 11 \\ 11 & 14\end{bmatrix}\](symmetric); A − A′ =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\](skew-symmetric). ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q9: find ½(A + A′) and ½(A − A′) for A =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & a & b \\ -a & 0 & c \\ -b & -c & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: A is already skew-symmetric: ½(A + A′) = O (zero matrix) and ½(A − A′) = A itself

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q10(i): write\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]as symmetric + skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: Symmetric part\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]skew part\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
It is already symmetric: symmetric part = A, skew part = O

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q10(iii):\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 & 1 \\ -4 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: Symmetric ½(A + A′) =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & \dfrac{1}{2} & -\dfrac{5}{2} \\[0.7em] \dfrac{1}{2} & -2 & -2 \\[0.7em] -\dfrac{5}{2} & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]skew ½(A − A′) =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & \dfrac{5}{2} & \dfrac{3}{2} \\[0.7em] -\dfrac{5}{2} & 0 & 3 \\[0.7em] -\dfrac{3}{2} & -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q10(iv):\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: Symmetric\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]skew\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term:
Ex 3.3 Q11: if A, B are symmetric of the same order, AB − BA is
(A) skew-symmetric
(B) symmetric
(C) zero
(D) identity
cards.definition: (AB − BA)′ = B′A′ − A′B′ = BA − AB = −(AB − BA): (A) skew-symmetric

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q12: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos  \alpha & -\sin  \alpha \\ \sin  \alpha & \cos  \alpha\end{bmatrix}\]and A + A′ = I. Then α = ?
cards.definition: A + A′ = 2 cos α · I = I so cos α = ½: (B) π/3

cards.term: Example 24: A, B symmetric. When is AB symmetric?
cards.definition: Exactly when AB = BA. (AB)′ = B′A′ = BA, which equals AB iff they commute

cards.term: Which of A + A′, A·A′, A′A are always symmetric for a square matrix A?
cards.definition: All three. (A + A′)′ = A + A′ (AA′)′ = (A′)′A′ = AA′ (A′A)′ = A′A. But AB for two symmetric matrices is not symmetric in general

cards.term: Misc Q1: A, B symmetric, prove AB − BA is skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: (AB − BA)′ = B′A′ − A′B′ = BA − AB = −(AB − BA). ✓

cards.term: Misc Q2: show B′AB is symmetric if A is symmetric and skew-symmetric if A is skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: (B′AB)′ = B′A′(B′)′ = B′A′B. If A′ = A it equals B′AB (symmetric); if A′ = −A it equals −B′AB (skew). ✓

cards.term: Define an invertible matrix and its inverse.
cards.definition:
A square matrix A of order n is invertible if ∃ a square matrix B of the same order with
AB = BA = I
Then B = A⁻¹

cards.term: Can a non-square matrix have an inverse?
cards.definition:
No.
AB and BA would need to be equal identities of the same order,
which forces A and B to be square of the same order

cards.term: The book’s example: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]and B =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]Are they inverses?
cards.definition: AB =\[\begin{bmatrix}4 - 3 & -6 + 6 \\ 2 - 2 & -3 + 4\end{bmatrix}\]= I and BA = I. So B = A⁻¹

cards.term: Inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
cards.definition: A^-1 = 1/(ad-bc) [[d,-b],[-c,a]]: swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal, divide by determinant; needs ad-bc != 0

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
2 × 2 inverse shortcut

Find the inverse of A = [[a, b], [c, d]] when ad − bc ≠ 0.

Swap the diagonal, flip the other two signs.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
2 × 2 inverse shortcut

Find the inverse of A = [[a, b], [c, d]] when ad − bc ≠ 0.

A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc)) [[d, −b], [−c, a]]: swap the diagonal, negate the other two entries, divide by ad − bc.

Example (the book’s A = [[2, 3], [1, 2]]): ad − bc = 1, so A⁻¹ = [[2, −3], [−1, 2]], and AA⁻¹ = I. If ad − bc = 0 there is no inverse. (The general method uses adjoints and determinants in Chapter 4.)

cards.term: Theorem 3: is the inverse of a matrix unique?
cards.definition: Yes. If B and C are inverses, B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C

cards.term: Theorem 4: (AB)⁻¹ = ?
cards.definition: B⁻¹A⁻¹: undo the last operation first. Proof: (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = AA⁻¹ = I. Similarly (ABC)⁻¹ = C⁻¹B⁻¹A⁻¹

cards.term: Relation between transpose and inverse: (A′)⁻¹ = ?
cards.definition: (A⁻¹)′, and (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A, (kA)⁻¹ = (1/k)A⁻¹ (k ≠ 0)

cards.term:
Ex 3.4 Q1: matrices A and B are inverses of each other only if
(A) AB = BA
(B) AB = BA = O
(C) AB = O, BA = I
(D) AB = BA = I
cards.definition: \[(D) AB = BA = I\]

cards.term: Which is true: AB = I ⇒ BA = I?
cards.definition: For square matrices of the same order, yes (a one-sided inverse is two-sided). This can fail for non-square matrices

cards.term: If A is invertible and AB = AC, what follows?
cards.definition: Multiply by A⁻¹: B = C. Invertibility restores the cancellation law that fails for singular matrices

cards.term: If AB = O and A is invertible, what is B?
cards.definition: B = A⁻¹(AB) = A⁻¹O = O

cards.term: Aⁿ for the rotation matrix is rotation by nθ
cards.definition: A = [[cos t, sin t],[-sin t, cos t]] rotates vectors clockwise by t; A^n = [[cos nt, sin nt],[-sin nt, cos nt]] (induction, Example 23)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Powers of a rotation matrix

A = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]] with θ = 30°. What does A do to the vector v = (1, 0)? What are A² and Aⁿ?

Follow the vector after each multiplication by A.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Powers of a rotation matrix

A = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]] with θ = 30°. What does A do to the vector v = (1, 0)? What are A² and Aⁿ?

A v = (cos θ, −sin θ): the vector is rotated clockwise by θ. Applying A twice rotates by 2θ, so Aⁿ = [[cos nθ, sin nθ], [−sin nθ, cos nθ]] (Example 23, proved by induction).

Check with the product formula: A·Aᵏ has entries cos θ cos kθ − sin θ sin kθ = cos (k + 1)θ and so on.

cards.term: Example 23: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos  \theta & \sin  \theta \\ -\sin  \theta & \cos  \theta\end{bmatrix}\]Prove Aⁿ =\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos  n\theta & \sin  n\theta \\ -\sin  n\theta & \cos  n\theta\end{bmatrix}\]for n ∈ N.
cards.definition: Induction: true for n = 1. If it holds for k, A^(k+1) = A·Aᵏ has top-left cos θ cos kθ − sin θ sin kθ = cos(k + 1)θ and top-right cos θ sin kθ + sin θ cos kθ = sin(k + 1)θ, etc. ✓

cards.term: Misc Q3: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2y & z \\ x & y & -z \\ x & -y & z\end{bmatrix}\]satisfies A′A = I. Find x, y, z.
cards.definition:
Columns must be orthonormal:
2x² = 1, 6y² = 1, 3z² = 1 (and the cross terms vanish)
x = ±1/√2, y = ±1/√6, z = ±1/√3

cards.term: Misc Q4: for what x is [1 2 1]\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\][0, 2, x]ᵀ = O?
cards.definition: Middle product = [4, x, 2x]ᵀ; then 4 + 2x + 2x = 0: x = −1

cards.term: Misc Q5: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]Show A² − 5A + 7I = O.
cards.definition:
A² =\[\begin{bmatrix}8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]5A =\[\begin{bmatrix}15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10\end{bmatrix}\]Entry by entry: 8 − 15 + 7 = 0, 5 − 5 = 0, −5 + 5 = 0, 3 − 10 + 7 = 0. ✓
Here tr A = 5 and det A = 7: A² − (tr A)A + (det A)I = O

cards.term: Misc Q6: find x if [x, −5, −1]\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\][x, 4, 1]ᵀ = O.
cards.definition: Middle product = [x + 2, 9, 2x + 3]ᵀ, then x(x + 2) − 45 − (2x + 3) = x² − 48 = 0: x = ±4√3

cards.term: Misc Q7: sales matrix: market I sells x, y, z as 10 000, 2 000, 18 000; market II as 6 000, 20 000, 8 000. Unit sale prices ₹2.50, ₹1.50, ₹1.00. Revenue in each market?
cards.definition: Multiply by the price column: I: 25 000 + 3 000 + 18 000 = ₹46 000; II: 15 000 + 30 000 + 8 000 = ₹53 000

cards.term: Misc Q7(b): unit costs ₹2.00, ₹1.00, ₹0.50. Gross profit?
Misc Q8: find X with\[X \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-7 & -8 & -9 \\ 2 & 4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: X is 2 × 2. Row 1: a + 4b = −7, 2a + 5b = −8, so a = 1, b = −2. Row 2: c + 4d = 2, 2c + 5d = 4, so c = 2, d = 0: X =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term:
Misc Q9: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}\alpha & \beta \\ \gamma & -\alpha\end{bmatrix}\]with A² = I. Then
(A) 1 + α² + βγ = 0
(B) 1 − α² + βγ = 0
(C) 1 − α² − βγ = 0
(D) 1 + α² − βγ = 0
cards.definition: A² = (α² + βγ) I, so α² + βγ = 1: (C)

cards.term:
Misc Q10: if A is both symmetric and skew-symmetric, then A is
(A) diagonal
(B) zero matrix
(C) square
(D) none
cards.definition: (B) zero matrix (it is square and diagonal too, but zero is the precise answer)

cards.term:
Misc Q11: A² = A, then (I + A)³ − 7A =
(A) A
(B) I − A
(C) I
(D) 3A
cards.definition: Aⁿ = A for all n ≥ 1: (I + A)³ = I + 3A + 3A² + A³ = I + 7A, so the expression is (C) I

cards.term: Idempotent, involutory and nilpotent matrices?
cards.definition:
Idempotent: A² = A
Involutory: A² = I
Nilpotent: Aᵏ = O for some k
Example:\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]is nilpotent (A² = O)

cards.term: Find\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]ⁿ.
cards.definition: Compute A², A³:\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]Pattern (by induction):\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & n \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Powers of a diagonal matrix diag(a, b)?
cards.definition: diag(aⁿ, bⁿ): multiply the diagonal entries separately (diagonal matrices multiply entrywise on the diagonal)

cards.term: Find A⁻¹ for A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]with the shortcut.
cards.definition: ad − bc = 4 − 6 = −2. A⁻¹ = (1/−2)\[\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]=\[\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\[0.7em] \dfrac{3}{2} & -\dfrac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: Number of 3 × 3 symmetric matrices with entries in {0, 1}?
cards.definition: Six free entries (diagonal 3 and above-diagonal 3): 2⁶ = 64

cards.term: Number of 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrices with entries in {−1, 0, 1}?
cards.definition: Diagonal is 0; three free entries above it, each with 3 choices: 3³ = 27

cards.term: Trace of a square matrix: tr(A + B), tr(kA), tr(AB) vs tr(BA)?
cards.definition:
tr A = sum of diagonal entries
tr(A + B) = tr A + tr B
tr(kA) = k tr A
tr(AB) = tr(BA) (even if AB ≠ BA)

cards.term: If A and B are 3 × 3 with AB = BA, expand (A + B)³.
cards.definition:
Only because they commute: A³ + 3A²B + 3AB² + B³.
Same for (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B² and A² − B² = (A − B)(A + B)

cards.term: If A² − A + I = O, what is A⁻¹?
cards.definition: Multiply A² − A + I = O by A⁻¹ (A is invertible, since A(A − I) = −I):\[A^{-1} = I - A\]

cards.term: If A is a 3 × 3 matrix with A² = O, what is (I + A)⁻¹?
cards.definition: (I + A)(I − A) = I − A² = I, so (I + A)⁻¹ = I − A

cards.term:
MCQ: if a matrix has 12 elements, the number of possible orders is
(a) 4 (b) 6 (c) 8 (d) 12
cards.definition: Divisor pairs of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 → (b) 6

cards.term:
MCQ: if A is 3 × 4 and B is 4 × 2, the order of AB is
(a) 3 × 2 (b) 4 × 4 (c) 2 × 3 (d) not defined
cards.definition: (a) 3 × 2

cards.term:
MCQ: if A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]and B =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]AB =
(a)\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}\](b)\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\](c)\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\](d)\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]
cards.definition: Multiplying by B on the right swaps the columns: (a)\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term:
MCQ: if A is a square matrix with A² = A, then (I + A)² =
(a) I + A (b) I + 2A (c) I + 3A (d) I − A
cards.definition: I + 2A + A² = I + 3A: (c)

cards.term:
MCQ: if A =\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta\end{bmatrix}\]then A² =
(a)\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos 2\theta & -\sin 2\theta \\ \sin 2\theta & \cos 2\theta\end{bmatrix}\](b)\[\begin{bmatrix}\cos ^{2}\theta & -\sin ^{2}\theta \\ \sin ^{2}\theta & \cos ^{2}\theta\end{bmatrix}\](c) I (d) 2A
cards.definition: Rotation by θ twice is rotation by 2θ: (a)

cards.term:
MCQ: the matrix\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 & -7 \\ -5 & 0 & 11 \\ 7 & -11 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]is
(a) symmetric (b) skew-symmetric (c) diagonal (d) scalar
cards.definition: Zero diagonal and aⱼᵢ = −aᵢⱼ: (b) skew-symmetric

cards.term:
MCQ: for a square matrix A, A + A′ is always
(a) skew-symmetric (b) symmetric (c) diagonal (d) identity
cards.definition: (b) symmetric

cards.term:
MCQ: if A is invertible, (A′)⁻¹ =
(a) A′ (b) (A⁻¹)′ (c) A (d) −A′
cards.definition: (b) (A⁻¹)′

cards.term:
MCQ: if A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]then A² =
(a) A (b) −A (c) I (d) O
cards.definition: (c) I. A is involutory

cards.term:
MCQ: the number of 2 × 2 matrices with entries from {0, 1} is
(a) 4 (b) 8 (c) 16 (d) 2
cards.definition: 2⁴ = (c) 16

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): if A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]the (1, 2) entry of A¹⁰⁰ is?
cards.definition: Aⁿ =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & n \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]so 100

cards.term: Integer answer: if A =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]the sum of the entries of A⁻¹ is?
cards.definition: ad − bc = 1, so A⁻¹ =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]Sum = 2 − 3 − 1 + 2 = 0

cards.term: Integer answer: how many 3 × 3 matrices with entries 0 or 1 are there with exactly two 1s?
cards.definition: Choose which 2 of 9 positions: ⁹C₂ = 36

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: if AB = O then A = O or B = O.
R: the product of two non-zero real numbers is non-zero.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A false, R true (d) Both false
cards.definition: (c): R is true for numbers, but matrices can be zero divisors: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]have AB = O

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: (AB)′ = A′B′ for all conformable A, B.
R: (AB)′ = B′A′.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) A false, R true (c) A true, R false (d) Both false
cards.definition: (b): the correct rule reverses the order, so A is false

cards.term: True/False: every diagonal matrix commutes with every square matrix of the same order.

False. Only scalar matrices commute with all matrices.

cards.term: 2-mark: if A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]find A′ and check (A′)′ = A.
cards.definition: A′ =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]and (A′)′ =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]= A. ✓

cards.term: 3-mark: express\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
cards.definition: P = ½(A + A′) =\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & \dfrac{5}{2} \\[0.7em] \dfrac{5}{2} & 3\end{bmatrix}\]Q = ½(A − A′) =\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & \dfrac{3}{2} \\[0.7em] -\dfrac{3}{2} & 0\end{bmatrix}\]A = P + Q

cards.term: 3-mark: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]Show A² − 2A − 3I = O and hence find A⁻¹.
cards.definition:
A² =\[\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]so A² − 2A − 3I = O.
Then A(A − 2I) = 3I, so
A⁻¹ = (1/3)(A − 2I) =\[(1/3) \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]

cards.term: 4-mark: if A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]and f(x) = x² − 5x − 2, find f(A).
cards.definition:
A² =\[\begin{bmatrix}7 & 10 \\ 15 & 22\end{bmatrix}\]
A² − 5A − 2I =\[\begin{bmatrix}7 - 5 - 2 & 10 - 10 \\ 15 - 15 & 22 - 20 - 2\end{bmatrix}\]= O
This is Cayley–Hamilton: tr A = 5, det A = −2

cards.term: 4-mark: A =\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]B =\[\begin{bmatrix}a & 1 \\ b & -1\end{bmatrix}\]and (A + B)² = A² + B². Find a and b.
cards.definition:
(A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², so we need AB + BA = O.
AB =\[\begin{bmatrix}a - b & 2 \\ 2a - b & 3\end{bmatrix}\]and BA =\[\begin{bmatrix}a + 2 & -a - 1 \\ b - 2 & 1 - b\end{bmatrix}\]
Entry (1, 2): 2 − a − 1 = 0 gives a = 1
Entry (1, 1): 2a − b + 2 = 0 gives b = 4
a = 1, b = 4

cards.term: Case-based: coordinates of triangle vertices are the columns of\[\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]Multiplying on the left by\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]does what?
cards.definition: It changes the sign of every y-coordinate: reflection in the x-axis. New vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, −3)
